clue.text: Angry young man told to go here?

definitions.text: Angry young man told to go here?

blocks.note: wild means furious, very angry

blocks.clueFragment: young man told to go here
blocks.note: from the famous advice 'Go west, young man', credited to Horace Greeley

explanation.surface: A furious youth is being told where he can go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Angry young man' looks like the stock phrase for a rebellious writer, but it splits: angry is the first word, and the young man is the one advised to head west.
explanation.definitionFit: The frontier of nineteenth-century America was where young men were urged to seek their fortune, so the whole clue points there.

clue.text: Leave one floored, forlorn, unheld, up gum tree - devastated!

annotation.answer: PULL THE RUG FROM UNDER ONE

indicators.note: something devastated is wrecked and broken up, so the preceding words are smashed and rebuilt

blocks.note: the four words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Someone abandoned and stranded up a tree, utterly devastated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up a gum tree' is a British idiom for being in trouble. The answer runs across 2, 13 and 26.
explanation.definitionFit: To pull the rug from under someone is an idiom for suddenly removing their support, knocking them flat in surprise.

clue.text: Keynes's poetic precursor

blocks.note: surface reading: a poet who came before the economist Keynes and inspired him
setter's reading: the poet whose name comes just before Keynes in the name of an English new town

explanation.surface: A poet who supposedly paved the way for the economist John Maynard Keynes.
explanation.walkthrough: Milton Keynes is a new town in Buckinghamshire, England; the poet's name literally precedes Keynes in it.
explanation.definitionFit: John Milton, author of Paradise Lost, is the poet, and his surname is the first half of the town name Milton Keynes.

clue.text: In 24 across - clear miss

indicators.note: one thing placed in another is enclosed by it, so the second piece sits inside the first

blocks.note: the entry at 24 across is a stake in poker
to clear a sum is to make it as net profit

explanation.surface: A cross-reference followed by what reads like a missed shot cleared away.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference points at the grid entry, not the whole answer it starts; a girl's name is often clued as miss.
explanation.definitionFit: Miss is a title for an unmarried girl, and Annette is a girl's given name, so it stands for one.

clue.text: Detected bipartite castaway

indicators.note: having two parts tells us the next word is to be split in two and each half rendered separately

blocks.note: to found metal is to cast it in a mould
away from home means out
the whole word is surface only; its two halves are the blocks

explanation.surface: Someone shipwrecked in two halves has been discovered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Castaway' looks like one word for a shipwrecked person; it must be split into cast and away.
explanation.definitionFit: Being found out means being discovered or exposed, the same sense as detected.

clue.text: Butter-fingered colt, as it were?

indicators.note: as it were hints the word is only loosely itself, handled clumsily so its letters slip out of place

blocks.note: someone butter-fingered keeps dropping things
taken as written

explanation.surface: A young horse that keeps dropping whatever it is given.
explanation.walkthrough: Fumble the letters of colt and you get clot, British slang for a fool, so a clumsy colt really is a clumsy clot.
explanation.definitionFit: A butter-fingered person is an awkward fool, which is exactly what the phrase describes in British slang.

clue.text: Roar of Saul, a literary lion

blocks.note: first meaning: a loud deep shout
second meaning: the Nobel-winning American novelist

explanation.surface: A literary lion lets out a roar.
explanation.walkthrough: A literary lion is a celebrated writer, so the lion's roar is a red herring; Saul Bellow wrote Herzog.
explanation.definitionFit: A bellow is a deep loud shout, and Saul Bellow was a famous novelist, so both senses share the spelling.

clue.text: See 24 across

definitions.note: a cross-reference instruction: this light holds the second part of the answer clued at 24 across

blocks.note: the last eight letters of the shuffle worked at 24 across

explanation.walkthrough: This light has no clue of its own; the clue at 24 across gives ANTEDILUVIAN, split across both lights.
explanation.definitionFit: Diluvian means relating to a flood, especially Noah's, and completes the adjective begun in the other light.

clue.text: Contrarily, Verne's captain enlisted 51 well-drilled personnel

indicators.note: going contrary means going the opposite way, so the name is read backwards
to enlist is to take into the ranks, so the captain's name takes in the number

blocks.note: Captain Nemo commands the Nautilus in Jules Verne's novel
51 in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Captain Nemo recruits a disciplined crew of fifty-one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Well-drilled' looks like praise for discipline, but these personnel literally drill wells.
explanation.definitionFit: Oilmen work in the petroleum business, whose workers bore wells into the ground for crude.

clue.text: Superstar left after wedding speech

indicators.note: following on means this piece is placed behind the other

blocks.note: the vow spoken at a wedding
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A celebrity walks out after giving a speech at a wedding.
explanation.definitionFit: An idol is someone hugely admired and adored by fans, which is what a superstar is.

clue.text: Noah's want, wet mobility, went adrift. So how did he pack them in?

annotation.answer: THE ANIMALS WENT IN TWO BY TWO

definitions.text: So how did he pack them in?

indicators.note: something adrift floats loose with no fixed position, so these letters are set free and rearranged

blocks.note: the five words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Noah, needing a way to get about in the wet, set off afloat and had to fit everyone aboard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Went' looks like part of 'went adrift' but belongs to the letters; only 'adrift' does the shuffling. The answer runs across 11, 12 and 14.
explanation.definitionFit: The line from the nursery song describes Noah boarding the creatures onto the ark in pairs, answering how he loaded them.

clue.text: See 11
See 2
See 11
No churchgoer is in at the Reformation!

indicators.note: one word sitting in the following phrase means it is placed inside
a re-formation is a forming again, so the letters are shaped anew

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone who skips church joins in during the Protestant Reformation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reformation' with its capital looks like the religious upheaval; here it simply means formed again.
explanation.definitionFit: An atheist rejects belief in God, so would hardly attend services; the phrase describes such a person.

clue.text: If it's right to go for Europe initially, it could be disaster for farming policy

indicators.text: right to go for Europe initially
indicators.note: one letter must leave so another can take its place, as the phrase 'go for' says
it could be signals that the letters might be arranged into something else

blocks.note: taken as written
R is the abbreviation for right
the opening letter of Europe

explanation.surface: A grumble that EU rules could ruin farming policy.
explanation.walkthrough: Set-aside was a European Community scheme paying farmers to leave land uncultivated.
explanation.definitionFit: Set-aside was the agricultural policy of paying farmers to take fields out of production to reduce surpluses.

clue.text: French production unit with English retail outlet

indicators.note: an outlet lets things out, so the word is let loose and rearranged

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for English
taken as written

explanation.surface: A French factory paired with an English shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retail outlet' reads as a shop, but 'outlet' is the shuffle signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Atelier is the French word for a workshop or studio where an artist or craftsman makes things.

clue.text: Still standing about mid-July, gets carried away

indicators.note: mid means only the middle of the month's name is wanted
about means going around, so the first word surrounds the second

blocks.note: extant means still in existence
the two central letters of July

explanation.surface: Something still standing in midsummer gets swept off.
explanation.definitionFit: Exultant means jubilant and elated, and being carried away is an idiom for being overcome by excitement.

clue.text: Could this be combined in his lover?

definitions.text: Could this be combined in his lover?

blocks.clueFragment: Could this be combined in his lover?
blocks.note: surface reading: whether some quality could be found united in a man's beloved
setter's reading: the words this and be run together make THISBE, the lover of the man we want

explanation.surface: Wondering whether all qualities might be united in one's beloved.
explanation.walkthrough: Pyramus and Thisbe are the doomed lovers of Ovid's tale, staged comically in A Midsummer Night's Dream.
explanation.definitionFit: In the classical story Thisbe is the beloved of the young Babylonian man who dies believing she was killed by a lion.

clue.text: Application for work

blocks.note: first meaning: diligence, hard steady effort
second meaning: manufacturing and commerce, the world of employment

explanation.surface: A job application form.
explanation.definitionFit: Industry means both diligent effort and the sector of economic activity where goods are produced.

clue.text: Fool might get up to act in lone parts

indicators.note: in a down entry rising means reading from the bottom upward
one item placed in another is enclosed by it
a word broken into parts is split and its letters regrouped

blocks.note: to do is to act
taken as written

explanation.surface: A fool may end up taking on solo roles in a play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Act' and 'parts' suggest theatre roles; act is just the verb do.
explanation.definitionFit: Noodle is an old informal word for a silly person or simpleton, and also slang for the head.

clue.text: A king's ransom, say?

definitions.note: the answer is the first name of the author whose surname sounds like ransom

blocks.note: first meaning: the legendary ruler of Camelot
second meaning: the given name of the author of Swallows and Amazons, Ransome

explanation.surface: A huge price demanded for a captured monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A king's ransom' is the stock phrase for a vast sum; split it, and the king and the Ransome share a first name.
explanation.definitionFit: The name belongs both to the British king of legend and to the children's novelist Arthur Ransome.

clue.text: Things to be done last as Miss Trollope's range goes out

indicators.note: going outside something means wrapping round it, so the cooker encloses the first piece

blocks.note: Joanna Trollope's novels were nicknamed Aga sagas, after the big stove of country kitchens
the last part is the end

explanation.surface: The final item as a novelist's cooking range finally goes cold.
explanation.walkthrough: An Aga is a cast-iron range cooker found in comfortable English farmhouse kitchens; Joanna Trollope's middle-class novels were dubbed Aga sagas.
explanation.definitionFit: Agenda is Latin for matters to be acted upon, and is now a list of items for a meeting.

clue.text: Appropriate factions warring in church

indicators.note: warring sides are in turmoil, so these letters are thrown into disorder
placed in means enclosed by the abbreviation that follows

blocks.note: CE stands for Church of England
taken as written

explanation.surface: Fitting that rival groups should be fighting inside a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Appropriate' reads as the adjective fitting; here it is the verb to seize.
explanation.definitionFit: To appropriate is to take possession of something, which is what an authority does when it seizes goods.

clue.text: Inundate vital disorder: no time before 11 12 14

indicators.note: disorder means messing up the arrangement of the preceding letters
no means without, so the letter for time is dropped

blocks.note: the two words taken letter for letter
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A flood causing a vital breakdown, with no time to spare.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged letters make ANTEDILUVIAN, entered as ANTE here and DILUVIAN at 8 across. 11 12 14 is Noah's ark story, so before it means before the Flood.
explanation.definitionFit: Antediluvian literally means from before the biblical Flood, when Noah loaded the ark with animals in pairs.

clue.text: Flower with attitude, say?

indicators.note: say asks us to speak the word and spell what we hear differently

blocks.note: an air is a manner or attitude, as in putting on airs

explanation.surface: A bloom that has a certain swagger about it.
explanation.walkthrough: Flower is crossword code for river, something that flows; the Aire runs through Leeds in Yorkshire.
explanation.definitionFit: The Aire is a river in Yorkshire, and a river is something that flows, hence a flower.

clue.text: Half in for a penny, in for a pound! It was in Essex once

indicators.note: half of a two-letter word keeps only its opening letter
the proverb's own words say the pound goes in

blocks.note: the opening half of in
L is the abbreviation for pound, from Latin libra
for taken as written with D, the old abbreviation for a penny

explanation.surface: The proverb about full commitment: once you have started, you might as well go all the way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In for a penny, in for a pound' means once committed, go all the way. Old British pennies were written d.
explanation.definitionFit: Ilford was an Essex town until 1965, when it was absorbed into the London Borough of Redbridge.

clue.text: See 2
